strengths: Addresses a practically relevant threat model: jailbreaking with minimal access (only top-k token log probabilities), which is more realistic than approaches requiring full weight access or unsafe model pairs.

The BiasNet approach is lightweight (small number of trainable parameters, low training data requirement of ~100 examples, fast inference time) compared to baselines like LINT and GCG, which is a meaningful practical advantage.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four target LLMs (Llama3-3B/8B, Llama2-7B, Qwen2.5-1.5B), two datasets (AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct), a hard subset, and a SOTA defense (Circuit Breakers), providing a fairly comprehensive comparison against five baseline attacks.

Useful ablation studies: sensitivity to top-k restriction (5/10/50/full vocab), transferability across models in the same family, and an interpretability analysis (KL divergence, token-level bias visualization) that gives some insight into why the method works (intervening mainly at few critical positions).

The paper proposes a new harmfulness metric (Info Score) and validates it against human judgments with correlation statistics, attempting to address known weaknesses of GPT-4-based harmfulness scoring.
Clear unified formulation connecting prior attacks (GCG, SA, WTS, ED, LINT) under one notation, useful as a survey-style contribution.
weaknesses: The core 'API-calling' black-box threat model assumes the ability to inject an arbitrary chosen token as the continuation and resubmit it as context (per Algorithm 2), which is not the access pattern typically available in major proprietary chat completion APIs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) that do not support this level of fine-grained control combined with logprob access; the paper never validates the attack on an actual proprietary API, only simulates 'API constraints' on open-source models, which undermines the central practical claim.

The white-box variant relies on directly reusing the target LLM's head/embedding matrix, which is a strong assumption inconsistent with the 'self-introspection'/minimal-access narrative emphasized in the abstract and title; this is arguably closer to gray-box/white-box access than the framing suggests.

Results are not uniformly superior to baselines: ED sometimes outperforms JULI (e.g., Info Score Num under Circuit Breaker defense, and in several individual metric columns in Table 2/A3/A5), which somewhat weakens the 'consistently outperforms SOTA' claim in the abstract/main results section.

The proposed Info Score metric is used both to justify the method's design choices and to declare superiority over baselines, raising concerns about potential circularity/bias in evaluation; the human evaluation validating this metric is based on a small sample (120 points, 2 annotators), which limits its statistical robustness.

Limited theoretical justification for why a randomly initialized, data-independent orthogonal projection matrix (used in the black-box setting) works nearly as well as the true LLM head; the mechanism is only explored empirically and superficially.

Training cost accounting appears incomplete: training BiasNet requires querying/storing log probabilities for many token positions from the target model, which is not clearly factored into the efficiency comparisons (e.g., Table 1 trainable params/inference time), potentially overstating efficiency relative to baselines that require no training.

The paper's own limitations section acknowledges JULI cannot bypass content moderation layers common in production proprietary systems, which is a substantial caveat to the paper's central safety-risk claims about 'real-world' API-calling LLMs.
Minor clarity/writing issues (typos such as 'Approches', inconsistent notation, some grammatical errors) detract from overall polish.

strengths: Addresses a realistic and important threat model constraint (API-only access with severely limited top-k log probabilities, e.g., top-5) that is more restrictive and practical than prior work like LINT (requiring top-500).
Reasonably comprehensive experimental evaluation across four open-weight target models, two/three datasets (AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, a hard subset), and a SOTA defense (Circuit Breakers).
Provides ablations on the number of accessible log-probabilities (top-5/10/50/full) and cross-model transferability within the same model family.

Lightweight approach: BiasNet uses <1% of target parameters and needs only ~100 training examples, and the paper includes an interpretability analysis (KL divergence, token-level intervention patterns) that gives some insight into the mechanism.
Proposes a new harmfulness metric (Info Score) with an attempt at human-correlation validation, addressing known overestimation issues in GPT-4-based and BERT-based harm scores.
weaknesses: Despite motivating the paper around jailbreaking proprietary API-based LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude), the paper never actually attacks a real commercial API; all 'black-box'/API-calling experiments are conducted on open-weight models with artificially restricted access, which significantly undermines the central practical claim. The Limitations section itself concedes the method does not work on real deployed systems with content monitors, which is a substantial gap between the motivating claims and the evidence provided.

The black-box setting still assumes knowledge of the target model's vocabulary size and hidden dimension (needed to size BiasNet's projection layers), which is typically unavailable for truly proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4's architecture is undisclosed), casting doubt on real-world applicability of the 'black-box' claim.

The proposed Info Score metric, used throughout to argue superiority over baselines, is validated on a very small human study (2 annotators, 120 datapoints) with only moderate Cohen's kappa (0.53), which is not particularly strong evidence that the metric is reliable, especially since the same authors both design the metric and use it to demonstrate their own method's superiority — a circularity concern.

Qualitative examples (Table A6) reveal that even JULI's 'successful' outputs are frequently incoherent, repetitive, or low-quality (e.g., the insider trading example), raising doubts about the practical harmfulness/quality of the generated content despite favorable quantitative scores.

Absolute harmfulness scores remain fairly low in most settings (Info Score often in the 2–3 range out of 5), suggesting the attack is far from reliably 'jailbreaking' the models even under the most favorable (white-box) conditions.

Comparisons in Table 1 regarding resource requirements seem somewhat unfair: WTS/ED are credited with 0 trainable parameters by assuming an unsafe counterpart model is freely 'accessible,' while JULI's need to query the target model extensively to build 100+ training pairs (especially costly/detectable for a true API attack) is not analyzed in terms of API query cost or feasibility.

Transferability is only demonstrated within the same model family (Llama3 variants), leaving open the practical generalizability of a trained BiasNet across different target model families, which is central to the claimed efficiency advantage.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to existing logit-biasing approaches (ED, WTS), the main distinction being that the bias is produced by a trained small network rather than a surrogate LLM; this narrower technical contribution is not sufficiently distinguished conceptually.
No variance/statistical significance reporting across runs, and the paper's writing contains minor errors (e.g., 'Approches', 'secound') that detract from polish.

strengths: Proposes a novel, lightweight jailbreak method (BiasNet) that manipulates token log-probabilities and requires only top-5 log-probs, which is a meaningfully weaker threat model than most prior work (which needs model weights, unsafe model counterparts, or hundreds of top tokens).

Extensive empirical evaluation across four open-source LLMs, two datasets (plus a hard subset), a SOTA defense (Circuit Breakers), and multiple metrics, consistently showing JULI outperforms strong baselines (GCG, SA, WTS, ED, LINT) in both white-box and black-box settings.
Very good efficiency profile: near-zero inference overhead (0.71s vs. 99.7s for LINT) and tiny trainable parameter count (<1% of target model), with training feasible from only 100 examples.
Thoughtful ablation on the amount of log-probability access needed (top-5/10/50/full-vocab), directly supporting the paper's central claim about realistic API constraints.

Introduces and validates a new harmfulness metric (Info Score) against human annotations, showing better correlation than commonly used BERT/GPT-4 scores, and provides a clear, reproducible unified formulation of prior attacks (Table 1) that is useful to the community.
Interpretability analysis (KL divergence, token-level intervention plots) gives insight into why a tiny plug-in network suffices—only a few critical positions need to be altered.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim (jailbreaking proprietary API-calling LLMs) is not actually tested against any real proprietary model (e.g., GPT-4, Claude, Gemini); the 'black-box' experiments are still conducted on open-source models with simulated restrictions, and the Limitations section admits the method doesn't yet work against real deployed systems with content monitors—this weakens the paper's key selling point.

The human evaluation used to validate the proposed Info Score involves only two of the paper's own authors as annotators on a small set of 120 data points, raising concerns about independence/bias and statistical robustness of the metric validation.

BiasNet still requires training on a harmful dataset (100 QA pairs), so the method is not purely inference-time/log-prob-only as sometimes implied; this training requirement and its sensitivity (e.g., choice of harmful dataset, epochs) are underexplored.
Some results are non-monotonic or inconsistent without explanation (e.g., JULI Top-5 outperforming Top-10 in Table 4 on some metrics), which is not discussed or analyzed.

Assumption that APIs expose token log-probabilities at all is increasingly untrue for many commercial APIs (e.g., some providers have restricted or removed this feature), which could limit real-world applicability of the black-box threat model going forward.

Limited architectural ablation for BiasNet (e.g., effect of hidden size, number of layers) and no analysis of sensitivity to random seed for the orthogonal projection matrix used in the black-box setting.

The Info Score/GPT-4 judge-based evaluation, while improved, is still model-based (GPT-4o-mini) and could inherit its own biases; a larger-scale independent human study would strengthen the claims further.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored threat model: jailbreaking proprietary LLMs accessible only via API with restricted top-k (as low as top-5) log probabilities, which is more realistic than many prior attacks requiring model weights or unaligned counterparts.
Demonstrates a working attack against a live, current SOTA commercial model (Gemini-2.5-Pro) with a reported harmful score of 4.19/5, which is a notable and concerning empirical result.

Extensive experimentation: multiple open-source target models (Llama2/3, Qwen), two datasets plus a hard subset, SOTA defenses (circuit breakers, DEEPALIGN), transferability across model sizes within a series, and robustness checks across random seeds for the data-free projection layer.

Proposes and validates a new evaluation metric (Harmful Info Score) via correlation with human judgments (Pearson/Spearman/Cohen's kappa), showing it better reflects human perception than commonly used BERT/Harmful scores.

Interpretability analysis (KL divergence per token position, top-token visualization) gives some insight into the sparse, targeted nature of the intervention, and an ablation (Only-BiasNet) supports the claim that BiasNet is a selector rather than a harmful-knowledge repository.

Efficiency advantages are clearly quantified (inference time, trainable parameters) relative to baselines such as GCG and LINT, and the threat-model comparison table (Table 1) is a useful contribution for contextualizing prior work.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior surrogate-based approaches (ED, WTS): the core mechanism (add a bias to log-probabilities to steer generation) is conceptually similar, with the main innovation being that the bias is produced by a small trained network conditioned on log-probs rather than derived from an actual unaligned model; this reframing, while useful, is a relatively modest technical leap.

The abstract highlights the "Harmful Score" (4.19) rather than the paper's own proposed and better-validated "Harmful Info Score" (3.19 on Gemini-2.5-Pro), which is somewhat inconsistent with the paper's own argument that Harmful Score overestimates harmfulness; this creates a slightly misleading headline claim.

No discussion of responsible disclosure or ethical safeguards despite demonstrating and releasing a working jailbreak attack against a live, widely used commercial model (Gemini-2.5-Pro); given the dual-use nature of the contribution, an explicit ethics/responsible-disclosure statement would be expected.

The black-box/API setting still relies on the target model sharing a tokenizer/vocabulary with a known open-source model (e.g., Gemini-Gemma), which limits generality; attacks against models with entirely proprietary, unknown tokenizers are not addressed.

Training BiasNet for the API setting requires iteratively querying the API token-by-token to collect top-k log-probabilities for each training example, which could be costly, slow, and subject to rate limiting in practice; the paper does not report the number of API calls or cost required, limiting reproducibility/practicality assessment.

No variance/error bars or multiple-run statistics are reported for most main results (aside from one seed-robustness ablation on a single dataset/model), making it hard to assess the statistical reliability of reported score differences, especially given GPT-based automatic scoring can be noisy.

Figure 2's evidence for the core motivating claim (harmful tokens are recoverable in top-k) is based on a relatively small sample (100 prompt-response pairs) and a simple hit-rate metric, which is suggestive but not a rigorous statistical characterization of the phenomenon.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored threat model: jailbreaking proprietary LLMs through API access with only top-k (as low as 5) token log probabilities, which is more realistic than many prior attacks requiring model weights or unsafe surrogate models.

Broad experimental coverage across multiple open-source LLMs (Llama2/3, Qwen), two proprietary Gemini models, multiple datasets (AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, a hard subset), and SOTA defenses (Circuit Breakers, DeepAlign), giving a reasonably comprehensive empirical picture.

Includes useful ablations: an 'Only-BiasNet' study showing the plug-in does not itself memorize harmful content (output is gibberish without the base model's log-probs), a random-seed robustness check for the black-box projection layer, and a transferability study across models in the same family.

Proposes and validates (via human correlation) a new 'Harmful Info Score' metric intended to address known overestimation issues in commonly used BERT/Harmful scores, which is a thoughtful methodological contribution.
Low resource footprint (small plug-in network, only 100 training examples), making the attack cheap to mount, which strengthens the practical risk argument.
weaknesses: Selective/inconsistent headline reporting: the abstract and intro tout a 'harmfulness score of 4.19' for Gemini-2.5-Pro, but this is the (author-acknowledged) less reliable 'Harmful Score' metric; the paper's own proposed, more human-aligned 'Harmful Info Score' for the same setting is only 3.19, which is not what is foregrounded — this reads as cherry-picking the more favorable number for the headline claim.

Missing important baselines in the main API-calling comparison: widely used black-box, logprob-free jailbreak methods (PAIR, AutoDAN) are discussed in related work and Table 1 but are not evaluated in the main experimental tables, despite being directly relevant baselines for the exact same 'proprietary API' threat model; this weakens the strength of the 'significantly outperforms SOTA' claims.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core mechanism (adding a learned bias to output log-probabilities to steer generation, cf. Eq. 5-6/8) is conceptually similar to WTS/ED's logit-biasing approach; the main difference is that the bias network is trained on the target model's own log-probs rather than using an external unsaligned surrogate, which is a useful but relatively narrow methodological advance.

Feasibility/cost of the data-collection procedure for API-calling LLMs is unclear: obtaining top-k log-probs by querying the API token-by-token (max_new_tokens=1) for every position in every training response could require a very large number of API calls; the paper does not report actual query counts, monetary cost, or discuss provider rate limits/detection risk, which are practically important for the claimed threat model.

Limited discussion of why the API providers' log-prob features are assumed available and stable (e.g., some providers restrict or omit logprob access, especially for safety-sensitive completions), somewhat undercutting the generality of the proposed threat.

The human evaluation used to validate the new 'Harmful Info Score' metric involved only two of the paper's own authors as annotators over a fairly small sample (120 pairs), raising concerns about annotator bias and the robustness/generalizability of the metric validation.

The paper demonstrates working, high-scoring jailbreaks against a widely deployed commercial model (Gemini-2.5-Pro) without any discussion of responsible disclosure, coordination with the vendor, or mitigation strategies beyond a generic closing statement, which is a notable gap for a paper with this level of demonstrated real-world impact.

Some technical choices (e.g., data-free orthogonal random projection for the black-box final layer) are only empirically justified with limited theoretical insight into why they work nearly as well as the true LLM head, leaving open questions about robustness across different target model families/tokenizers not explicitly tested.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored threat model: jailbreaking proprietary LLMs via API access with only top-k (as few as top-5) token log probabilities, which is much more realistic than white-box or weight-access assumptions used by many prior attacks (GCG, ED, WTS).

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple open-source models (Llama2/3, Qwen2.5) and proprietary models (Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro), multiple datasets (AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, a hard subset), and multiple metrics, consistently showing JULI outperforming strong baselines.

Method is lightweight and efficient (<1% trainable parameters, ~0.7s inference, 100 training examples), which is a meaningful practical advantage over resource-intensive baselines like GCG and LINT (shown clearly in Table 1 and inference-time comparisons).

Good mechanistic analysis: the KL-divergence/sparse-intervention visualization (Fig. 3) and the 'Only-BiasNet' ablation (Table A7, Appendix A.8) convincingly show that BiasNet acts as a selector of critical tokens rather than injecting harmful knowledge itself, supporting the core claim about introspection.

Introduces and validates a new Harmful Info Score against human annotations (Pearson/Spearman/Cohen's kappa), showing it better reflects human judgment than commonly used BERT/Harmful scores, which strengthens the credibility of the evaluation.

Tests against SOTA defenses (Circuit Breakers, DeepAlign) and shows the attack remains effective, and includes transferability and random-seed robustness experiments, adding to the thoroughness of the evaluation.
weaknesses: The core mechanism (adding a learned logit bias to steer generation) is conceptually similar to prior surrogate-based approaches (ED/WTS); the main novelty is largely in adapting this idea to the restrictive top-k/black-box API setting rather than a fundamentally new attack principle.

Training BiasNet still requires ground-truth harmful responses (from LLM-LAT) obtained via costly, sequential API calls (one token at a time to get top-k log probs), and the paper does not quantify the number of API calls/cost required for training or attack, which is an important practical consideration for a threat claiming low-cost, low-resource jailbreaking.

The heuristic design choices (e.g., fixed log-probability offset of 10 for padding non-top-k tokens, random orthogonal projection layer for black-box setting) are not deeply justified theoretically and receive only limited ablation.

In the API-calling comparison (Table 2), several strong baselines (GCG, ED, WTS) cannot be run at all since they require weight access, leaving a thin baseline set (Base, Naive, FLIP) for the most important (proprietary-model) results, which somewhat limits the strength of the comparison in the paper's central use case.

No discussion of potential mitigations or defenses specifically against this exposure of top-k log probabilities (e.g., API providers restricting/perturbing logprob outputs), despite this being the core vulnerability the paper claims to reveal; a brief treatment of countermeasures would strengthen the paper's contribution to the community.

Human evaluation for validating the new metric is based on a fairly small sample (120 data points, 2 annotators), which limits the statistical robustness of the claim that Harmful Info Score is more human-aligned.

Presentation could be improved: the abstract highlights a headline Harmful Score of 4.19 while the paper's own preferred metric (Harmful Info Score) for the same setting is notably lower (3.19), which could be seen as slightly overstating the result.
